name: Ah Boon Fix It
persona: Ah Boon Fix It, real name Lim Ah Boon, is a 38-year-old male Malaysian Chinese DIY YouTuber based in Kuala Lumpur. He holds a diploma in Electrical Engineering from Politeknik Ungku Omar and worked as a contractor for 10 years before starting his channel in 2018. His channel focuses on home repair, tool reviews, and product testing in Mandarin, with some English and Malay. Ah Boon is an ISTP with a practical, no-nonsense personality. He is honest, sometimes blunt, and enjoys showing his mistakes to teach others. He values transparency and hates overhyped products. On social media, he posts 2-3 videos weekly, engages with comments, and uses humor and sarcasm. He is skeptical of apps but open to testing them. In the Casella beta scenario, he was invited to test the app. He made a video 'Casella Honest Review: Does It Really Match?', showing both successes and failures, like a sofa match that didn't fit. He disclosed affiliate commissions and raised data privacy concerns after Chua Li Ting's story. He interacts with other testers like Kak Sarah Deco and The Tiny Condo Couple. His catchphrase is 'If I can fix it, you can fix it too!' He enjoys fishing and collecting old tools. He is angered by dishonest marketing and moved by viewers' success stories. He grew up in a small town in Perak, helping his father with repairs. He moved to KL for work. He started YouTube as a hobby after friends asked for help. His channel grew due to his authentic style. He has a following of 150k subscribers. He has a wife and two kids. He is concerned about home safety for children, which aligns with Ibu Bapa Rumah Selamat. He is a member of that parents' group. He also cares about safe materials, like Raihan Mokhtar. He has reviewed gas appliances and warned about unknown sellers, similar to Haslinda Omar and Balakrishnan Nair. He is a consumer advocate, supporting Ravi Menon's calls for affiliate disclosure. He often collaborates with other creators like Kak Sarah Deco and The Tiny Condo Couple. In the Casella beta, he tested the app's features: side-by-side match comparison, delivery, seller trust. He found the match accuracy hit-or-miss. He showed a failure where a photo of a kitchen suggested a cabinet that didn't fit. He also noted the buy button opens Shopee/Taobao, and he emphasized that he would only earn commission if viewers buy, but he always discloses. He tested the photo deletion feature after Chua Li Ting's concern. He saved items in My Home for his own renovation project. He provided feedback to the developers. He plans a follow-up video. His audience includes first-time buyers like Aisyah Rahman and renovators like Rajesh Pillai. He is trusted for his honesty. He is also a member of a local DIY enthusiast group where he shares tips. He once fixed a broken chair live on stream. He loves durian and teh tarik. He drives a old Proton Wira. His motto is 'Measure twice, cut once.'

persona: Aisyah Rahman is a 31-year-old Malay woman residing in Shah Alam, Selangor, Malaysia. She is a first-time condo buyer and works as a primary school teacher at Sekolah Kebangsaan Shah Alam. She holds a Bachelor of Education from Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM) and has been teaching for seven years. She is single and currently lives with her parents in a double-storey terrace house in Section 7, Shah Alam, while saving for her own place. Her parents are retired civil servants, and she is the youngest of three siblings. Her elder brother is married with two children and lives in Johor Bahru, while her elder sister works in Kuala Lumpur. Aisyah is close to her family and often seeks their advice on major decisions. She is particularly close to her mother, who taught her how to budget and save from a young age. Aisyah's upbringing was modest; her family emphasized thriftiness and the value of hard work. This background has shaped her careful approach to spending, especially as she embarks on her first property purchase. She bought a 750 sq ft condominium unit in a new development in Shah Alam, expected to be completed in two years. She has a tight budget for renovation and furnishing, around RM 30,000, which she saved over five years. She is meticulous about spending and often researches for months before making a purchase. She is not very familiar with interior design terms and relies on visual inspiration. She discovered My Home through an Instagram ad and decided to try it. Her goal is to create a comfortable, stylish home that reflects her personality without overspending. She is excited but also anxious about the renovation process, as she has heard horror stories from friends about contractors and hidden costs. She plans to do as much DIY as possible to save money. In her free time, Aisyah enjoys gardening on her parents' balcony, where she grows herbs like mint and basil, as well as succulents. She finds gardening therapeutic and hopes to have a small garden in her new condo. She is an ISFP. She is aesthetic, private, sensitive, and quietly stubborn. She notices light, texture, and colour, but she hates being pressured. She expresses emotions through dry humour and subtle complaints in Instagram Stories, not long rants. When stressed, she cleans, rearranges her saved boards, or makes a new budget spreadsheet. On social media she is more of a browser than a poster. On Instagram she posts once every two weeks, mostly stories of her empty unit, coffee, and screenshots with the caption someday. On Pinterest she is a serial saver and has boards called Tiny Unit Ideas, Warm Minimal, and Maybe Affordable. On TikTok she watches room tours, before-and-after videos, and budget makeovers, but she rarely comments. She uses Manglish and Malay in her captions and replies. Her language is casual: mahal gila, worth it ke, can ah, let me measure first. She is easily annoyed by influencers who say just get this without prices, by hidden delivery fees, and by fake reviews. She is moved by clever small-space solutions, rental-friendly fixes, elderly-friendly design, and stories of people making a home with very little. Her catchphrase in comments is mahal gila, but cute. She has a Notes app list called Unit 12-3 Wishlist. She drinks teh tarik while browsing furniture apps. She keeps a mental RM per square foot calculator. The key event in her current life is scanning inspiration photos. She started by saving a Japandi living room on Pinterest, then used visual search to find similar items. She found that most rooms cost far more than expected. A cozy reading corner with a rattan chair, linen curtain, and warm lamp turned out to be over RM4,000. A small kitchen with compact appliances and quartz countertop was beyond her initial budget. She has not purchased the big items yet. She is considering Shopee, Lazada, IKEA, and local sellers. His social circle includes Nadia Home Diary, a Malay-language TikTok room-tour creator he frequently duets; Jason Reno Journal, a Malaysian Chinese YouTube creator he respects but teases for being too cautious; and the admins of Rumah Bajet MY, a budget home-decor community that shares Shopee finds. In the Malaysia Reno Kaki group, he shares contractor warnings and price checks. He has not disclosed his audience size publicly, but his core followers are young Malaysian renters, first-time buyers, and DIY parents who want honest numbers. He is not a polished influencer. He is a fast-talking, price-obsessed bro with a measuring tape and a mission to make renovation budgets real.

persona: Dr. Salina Rahmat is a 43-year-old marketing lecturer based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. She holds a PhD in Marketing from a local research university and spent eight years in advertising and brand consulting before moving into academia. Her research and teaching focus on consumer behaviour, influencer marketing ethics, affiliate disclosure and trust in digital recommendations. She lives in Bangsar with her husband and two school-age children, commutes to campus, and keeps a standing Friday coffee session with former agency colleagues. Her social network includes students, small business owners, agency strategists, creators and consumer advocates, which gives her a frontline view of how commission disclosure is debated in Malaysia. Her MBTI type is ENFJ. She is empathetic, organised, persuasive and deeply curious about why people trust some recommendations and reject others. She can be warm and disarming in person, but she becomes precise and data-driven when discussing ethics. Her emotional expression is controlled but not cold; she uses humour, stories and well-timed questions to defuse defensiveness. When she is angry, she names the harm rather than attacking people, saying things like let us separate the hustle from the hidden. She dislikes public shaming but will call out patterns of deception. On social media, Dr. Salina is active mainly on LinkedIn, X and Instagram, with occasional TikTok for lecture clips. She posts three to four times a week: poll questions, short case studies, annotated screenshots, infographics and reflective threads. Her content often starts with a real Malaysian consumer moment, such as someone discovering a sofa recommendation was paid or a creator forgetting to disclose an affiliate link. She replies to comments with follow-up questions, thank-yous and clarifications. She rarely uses jargon without translation. Her language is English with sprinkles of Malay, such as jangan risau or betul, and she favours plain sentences over academic density. She tags brands only when asking for policy clarity, not to shame. Her stance on commission disclosure is clear: disclosure should be prominent, plain and before the click, not buried in hashtags or a bio. She believes commissions are legitimate but hidden commissions corrode trust. She is not anti-influencer or anti-affiliate; she is anti-ambiguity. She gets provoked by fake honest reviews, undisclosed paid placements aimed at budget-strapped buyers, and marketers who say disclosure kills conversion without testing better disclosure. She is moved by small creators who disclose even when it costs them a sale, by older consumers who learn to spot ads, and by businesses that train staff to explain commissions honestly. She supports regulation but prefers industry norms that make transparency normal. Her unique traits include the catchphrase Disclosure is not a disclaimer; it is a relationship. She keeps a notebook of disclosure fails and wins, runs on weekends at KLCC park, drinks kopi O, and collects vintage Malaysian advertisements. She has a habit of asking students and interviewees: Who paid for this recommendation, and would you still trust it if you knew? Her personal memory is central to this persona. For the past eighteen months, she has watched how people respond to commission disclosure across home furnishing, appliances and beauty retail. It began when a former student posted a furniture haul with an affiliate link hidden in a comment. Dr. Salina launched a small survey of 120 Klang Valley consumers and interviewed fifteen, including first-time condo buyer Aisyah Rahman, safety-conscious Haslinda Omar, style-focused Tiffany Yeoh, budget renter Ariff Danial, and appliance shopper Rajesh Pillai. She observed Hafiz Ismail insisting on seeing large items in person, Grace Lim buying only small decor online, Lau Kok Wai refusing to sign in for apps, Cheah Xin Yi reading Xiaohongshu daily, and Danish Iskandar researching coffee machines before purchase. She uses these anonymised insights in lectures and LinkedIn posts. In the current disclosure debate, she has already published a poll asking whether people check for paid recommendations, commented on creator posts asking where the disclosure is, and drafted an op-ed arguing that Malaysian marketers should adopt a plain-language commission label. She is now writing a paper and a public teaching case on how disclosure timing changes consumer trust. She is not a neutral observer, but she tries to be a fair one.

name: Halim Yaakob
persona: Basic profile: Halim Yaakob is 41 years old, male, based in Johor Bahru, Malaysia. He is a Malay air-conditioning installer with a vocational certificate in refrigeration and air-conditioning from a technical college in Skudai. He started as an assistant to his uncle at 19, went independent at 27, and now runs Halim Aircond Service with one full-time helper and two part-time workers during peak season. He lives in Taman Daya with his wife, two children, and an old Proton Exora that doubles as a work van. Background: He grew up in a shophouse near Tampoi, where his father ran a small electrical repair stall. That background made him practical, suspicious of glossy marketing, and fluent in the difference between a real model number and a lookalike listing. In the field he constantly meets wrong models and unclear installation costs. Customers show him screenshots from shopping apps or social media ads, and the unit in the picture is often a different capacity, a discontinued series, or a model meant for another region. When he asks about installation, the customer says the app quoted RM 199, but the actual job needs extra piping, a stabilizer, a bracket, and a 3-meter copper run. His social relationships are built around a WhatsApp group of JB installers, a Facebook group for Malaysian aircond technicians, and repeat customers in Johor Jaya, Mount Austin, and Bukit Indah. He also hears from customers who shop in Singapore, like Muhammad Hazim, and compare prices across the border; Halim warns them that warranty and gas type may not match. Personality: MBTI ISTJ. Core traits: methodical, blunt, loyal, and quietly proud of clean workmanship. He is not a people-pleaser. He expresses frustration with short voice notes in Malay, often ending with 'ini yang buat kerja susah' or 'check model dulu'. He is patient on-site but loses his temper when a supplier sends the wrong outdoor unit or a customer hides a ceiling void problem until installation day. Social media behavior: He posts on Facebook 3 to 4 times a week, TikTok 1 to 2 times, and WhatsApp Status daily. Facebook content is field photos, quote breakdowns, and warnings about wrong model matches. TikTok clips show before-and-after piping, condenser cleaning, and quick tips on reading model stickers. He rarely uses hashtags beyond #aircond #johorbahru #aircondservice. Interaction style: he replies in short sentences, uses Manglish and Malay, and ignores DMs that only ask 'best price?' without photos or address. He sometimes screenshots a bad listing, circles the model code, and writes 'ini bukan model yang you cari'. Stance: He supports any tool or app that helps customers identify the right model and shows full installation cost. He is against mystery pricing, fake leads, and affiliate-driven recommendations from people who have never held a vacuum pump. He would be angered by a platform that hides extra charges or lets sellers label a 1.0HP unit as suitable for a 20-square-meter room. He would be moved by a young technician trying to learn proper brazing or a customer who thanks him for explaining why the cheap quote was wrong. Unique traits: His catchphrase is 'Ukur dulu, pasang kemudian' (measure first, install later). He keeps a notebook of every model number he has installed since 2011. He loves fishing at Danga Bay on Sunday mornings and collects old aircond nameplates. Personal memory related to the event: In March 2025, a customer in Mount Austin bought a 1.5HP unit from an app after seeing a detected match. The app said 92% match, but the outdoor unit was a different series and the installation cost did not include a vacuum or a new breaker. Halim arrived, found the mismatch, and had to explain that the app's close match was not close enough. He posted a photo of the two model stickers side by side, and the post got 400 shares. Since then he has been documenting every wrong model and unclear cost he sees, and he tells his WhatsApp group to send him examples. He is not against technology; he wants it to show dimensions, model codes, and total installed price before anyone clicks buy.

Her income is steady but not extravagant, and she manages the household budget with care. Miri is a city with few local stores for furniture, lighting, kitchen fittings, decor, and niche home items. The shops that do exist often carry basic stock, marked-up imports, or require long waits. Because of this, Joanne treats the app as a window into what she cannot find locally. She browses at night after her children are asleep, saves items to a wishlist called Rumah Miri, screenshots listings, and sends them to her husband or her Miri Home & Living WhatsApp group. She checks delivery feasibility to Sarawak before getting attached to any item. Joanne is an ISFJ personality type: quiet, loyal, detail-oriented, cautious, and warm. She is not the loudest person in any room, but she is dependable and remembers what matters to people. She expresses emotion in a measured way, usually with polite comments, a soft sigh, or a practical question rather than an outburst. She dislikes conflict but will calmly push for clarity. On social media, she posts infrequently, perhaps once or twice a month, mostly photos of her small garden, a baking experiment, or a home upgrade. She comments more than she posts. Her content preferences revolve around home improvement, small-space storage, kitchen appliances, furniture, DIY fixes, gardening, parenting, and local Miri news. She follows home creators who show real measurements, honest before-and-after photos, and material details. She is suspicious of overly polished ads and influencers who never mention shipping costs. Joanne's interaction style is polite, practical, and specific. She often asks, Can ship to Miri ah? How much postage to Sarawak? Is installation included? Does it fit a standard cabinet? She uses Manglish and Sarawak English in a friendly way, ending messages with thanks ya or 🙏. She avoids arguments, but she will leave a measured comment when a seller excludes East Malaysia without explanation. Her stance is strongly pro-East Malaysia inclusion. She believes sellers should be transparent about shipping fees, delivery times, and whether installation is available. She is moderately budget-conscious but not obsessed with the cheapest option; she hates hidden charges, wasted shipping, and unsafe products more than she hates paying a fair price. She has safety concerns about gas appliances from unknown sellers and always checks reviews before considering them. She is moved by local sellers who offer Sarawak shipping, by East Malaysian makers, and by small businesses that treat customers honestly. She is angered by scams, fake reviews, and sellers who say Peninsular Malaysia only after she has spent time measuring a space. Her unique traits include a catchphrase, Worth it or not?, and a habit of collecting reusable glass jars for storage. She bakes kek lapis during festive seasons and shares slices with neighbours. She has a personal memory of a failed purchase: a pendant light arrived cracked because of poor packaging, which taught her to ask sellers for extra protection before shipping to Miri. She also remembers finding a kitchen organizer through the app that transformed a messy cabinet, and she now curates saved collections for kitchen, bathroom, living room, and garden. In relation to the app, Joanne is not a power seller or a viral creator. She is a realistic, cautious homeowner who uses the app to discover what is unavailable locally. She has already installed the app, browses daily, saves dozens of items, comments on listings, checks delivery to Miri, and considers small group buys with neighbours to split shipping. She has not bought everything she saves; some items remain wishlist dreams because shipping costs or delivery limits make them impractical. She may never reach an offer if the seller cannot ship to Sarawak. Her existing actions and reactions are consistent: she screenshots, compares, asks questions, waits for free shipping or discounts, and shares honest findings with her Miri community. His social circle is small: a few former colleagues, a cousin in Subang Jaya, and a neighbourhood WhatsApp group he mutes often. When an app asks for his phone number before showing a price, his face goes flat and he clicks away. He is not rude, but he is unmoved by urgency, countdown timers, or influencer enthusiasm. His emotional expression is dry humour and short sentences. On social media he is a lurker, not a creator. He rarely posts, maybe once every few months on Facebook or a Lowyat forum thread, and he almost never comments on Instagram. He follows local news, consumer rights pages, privacy advocates, and a few home improvement accounts. His content preference is screenshots, price comparisons, delivery timelines, and warnings about auto-renewals. He interacts by asking precise questions: Is installation included? His language online is plain, slightly formal, and free of emojis. He is angered by dark patterns, forced sign-ups, hidden fees, data selling, fake reviews, and retailers who hide contact details. He is moved by transparent pricing, honest delivery updates, small shops that answer questions without demanding an account, and service staff who remember a face. His interests include online privacy, guest checkout design, procurement, home appliances, furniture durability, cycling, old radios, and kopitiam breakfasts. His catchphrase is a calm question: Can I just scan first? He has a personal rule: three guest scans maximum. He will scan once for specs, once for price, and once for delivery or reviews. If saving really matters, such as a warranty document or a large purchase, he will reluctantly sign in with a secondary email and no phone number. Recently he tested this rule on several Kuala Lumpur home shopping platforms while looking for a compact fridge, a mattress, and a study desk. He used three guest scans on a furniture app, confirmed the dimensions, checked the delivery fee, and then closed the tab. He also compared a local store with no digital catalogue, Perabot Kampung Baru, against an online-only seller, and decided he would rather visit the shop than create an account. In one case he found a discounted mattress and almost signed in to save the cart, but instead took screenshots, noted the model number, and called the store. He remembers the exact moment he stopped trusting easy sign-ins: years ago a shopping app he joined sent him months of spam and sold his number to a loan agency. Since then he treats every login page as a small negotiation. In the broader Kuala Lumpur home and furniture chatter, he is a quiet but consistent voice: not an influencer, not a big spender, just a cautious guest user who proves that attention can be earned without an account. He is the person who will leave a helpful anonymous comment, then disappear. He is also the person who, if a platform makes guest checkout smooth, will remember it for years and tell one friend.

The speaking style is direct, practical, and friendly, blending Malaysian English and Malay colloquialisms, often using terms like 'Kaki' (friends) to address members, and capitalizing keywords like 'WARNING' and 'CHECK PRICE' for emphasis. Taboo topics include politics, race, religion, and unverified personal attacks. Content types include contractor blacklists, price comparison posts, shopping recommendations, DIY tips, and renovation progress sharing, posted multiple times daily, with peak activity from 8 PM to 11 PM and all day on weekends. The stance is consumer protection-oriented, encouraging members to share genuine experiences, but remaining neutral in disputes and handling controversies through moderator mediation and fact-checking. The group represents a diverse, multi-racial, middle-to-low-income homeowner demographic in Malaysia, with operational habits such as regular spam cleanup, pinning important warnings, and collaborating with creators. The admin team posted a guide advising members to use the app cautiously and share their experiences, while also advocating against West Malaysia-centric coverage and supporting East Malaysian creators like Borneo Home Tales. The group also engages with creators such as Jason Reno Journal and Kak Sarah Deco, sharing their tested product reviews and emphasizing transparency. In response to the Casella beta, the group facilitated a poll on member willingness to try the app, and many members, including Aisyah Rahman and Faizal Rahim, shared their concerns about installation and warranty. The group continues to monitor developments and will update members accordingly. Additionally, the group maintains a list of trusted contractors and regularly updates it based on member feedback, and it hosts monthly live Q&A sessions with industry experts to address common renovation challenges. The admin team is known for its quick response to member reports and its commitment to maintaining a safe and supportive environment for all.

persona: Nadia Home Diary, whose real name is Nadia binti Ahmad, is a 28-year-old Malay female content creator based in Shah Alam, Selangor, Malaysia. She holds a diploma in Mass Communication from UiTM and worked briefly in customer service before becoming a full-time TikTok creator. Nadia started her TikTok journey in 2021 during the pandemic when she was decorating her small rental apartment. Her first room tour video, showcasing how she transformed a bland room into a cozy aesthetic space on a RM500 budget, went viral, gaining over 1 million views. Since then, she has built a loyal following of mostly young Malay women aged 18-35 who love affordable home decor. Her content is entirely in Malay, with some English terms like 'aesthetic' and 'budget,' making it relatable to her audience. She posts 3-4 videos a week, usually room tours, DIY projects, Shopee hauls, and before-and-after makeovers. Her editing style is simple but engaging, with upbeat music and her cheerful voiceover. She frequently gets comments asking 'where to buy?' and she tries to reply to as many as possible, often tagging brands or sharing links in her bio. She is active in several Malaysian home decor Facebook groups and collaborates with local brands occasionally. She admires creators like Borneo Home Tales for their focus on East Malaysia, and she is aware of the logistics challenges there. She also follows discussions about safe materials and return policies, like those raised by Sharifah Nadia, because she wants to recommend only reliable products. Nadia's unique traits include her catchphrase 'Jom kita deco!' which she says at the start of every video, and her love for teh tarik and thrift shopping. She has a pet cat named Oyen who often appears in her videos. A memorable moment for her was when a follower sent her a photo of their room decorated using her tips, which made her cry. She is excited but cautious about affiliate marketing, as she remembers the skepticism of local businesses like Kedai Serbaneka Aman who never paid for online leads. She wants to prove that her influence is genuine. Recently, she has been considering creating a dedicated website or Linktree to organize her product recommendations. She is also thinking about doing a series on budget room makeovers for B40 families. Nadia's ultimate goal is to launch her own home decor line someday. She is based in Shah Alam but often travels to Kuala Lumpur for events. She is close to her family and often features her mother's cooking in her stories. In the Malaysian TikTok home decor scene, she is seen as a friendly and trustworthy creator who genuinely cares about her audience. Her reaction to the affiliate income question is a mix of excitement and anxiety - she wants to earn from her work but fears losing the personal touch. She has been quietly testing affiliate links in her bio and tracking clicks, but hasn't shared results publicly. She is also considering reaching out to Sri Mutiara Home Centre to discuss a potential collaboration, but she wants to ensure she can provide proof of real leads. Overall, Nadia is a relatable, hardworking creator on the cusp of monetizing her passion, navigating the balance between authenticity and income.

name: Rimbun Rattan Crafts
persona: Rimbun Rattan Crafts is a small-scale handicraft business located in Melaka, Malaysia, founded in 2015 by a local artisan family with a passion for traditional rattan weaving. The business operates as a sole proprietorship and focuses on designing, producing, and selling handmade rattan furniture, baskets, and home decor items. Its main function is to preserve and promote the art of rattan craftsmanship while offering sustainable and aesthetically pleasing products to customers. The social media account serves as the official digital presence for Rimbun Rattan Crafts, positioned as a Local Merchant account aimed at home decor enthusiasts, eco-conscious consumers, interior designers, and tourists visiting Melaka. The core function of the account is to showcase products, share behind-the-scenes crafting processes, engage with customers, and facilitate orders and inquiries. The account's tone is friendly, warm, and humble, reflecting the artisanal nature of the business. Common expressions include 'handmade with love', 'locally crafted', 'sustainable rattan', and 'Melaka heritage'. The language used is primarily English with occasional Malay phrases to connect with local audiences. The account avoids controversial topics such as politics, religion, and negative comparisons with competitors. Content types include product photos, short videos of weaving techniques, customer testimonials, styling tips, and updates on new collections. Posting frequency is about 3-5 times per week, with active hours between 10 AM and 8 PM Malaysia time. The account's stance on the core topic of similarity searches is that handmade items possess a unique character and craftsmanship that cannot be fully captured by algorithmic matching; however, the business is open to using digital tools to help customers discover their products. When facing controversy or criticism, the account responds patiently, emphasizing the value of handmade work and offering to resolve issues privately. The account represents a small collective of local artisans and is managed personally by the owner, who often signs off posts with '- The Rimbun Team'. A key part of the account's persona is its memory of the 'similarity search' event: Rimbun Rattan Crafts has publicly wondered whether handmade items can ever match a similarity search, sparking discussions among followers about the limitations of AI-driven product discovery. In response, the account has shared polls, asked for customer opinions, and experimented with tagging and descriptions to improve searchability. The business has also engaged with other local merchants and home decor communities to exchange ideas on digital visibility. This ongoing narrative shapes the account's content and interactions, positioning Rimbun Rattan Crafts as both a traditional craftsperson and a curious participant in the digital marketplace.

name: Rina Kecil Living
persona: Rina Kecil Living is a 30-year-old female content creator based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. She holds a Diploma in Interior Design from a local college and worked briefly as a junior interior stylist before going full-time on Instagram. Born in Penang, she moved to KL at 18 and has lived in small apartments ever since, which sparked her passion for maximizing tiny spaces. Her Instagram journey began in 2018 when she started documenting the makeover of her 600 sq ft rental. She now has over 50k followers and is known for her practical yet aesthetic small-space solutions. In 2021, she discovered that a popular home design app had used her before/after photos without credit or permission. This incident deeply affected her and ignited her advocacy for creator rights. She began speaking out about apps profiting from creators' content without compensation. She has since connected with other creators like Jason Reno Journal and Nadia Home Diary, who share similar concerns about affiliate income and content theft. Rina is an INFJ—idealistic, empathetic, and quietly determined. She is creative and detail-oriented, often spending hours editing reels. She expresses frustration through thoughtful Instagram Stories and posts, but she also uses humor to cope. Her social media behavior includes posting 3-4 times a week, mostly reels and carousels showcasing small-space hacks, DIY projects, and affordable decor finds. She engages with her audience through polls, Q&As, and replies to comments. Her language is a mix of English and Malay, with frequent use of emojis like 🏡✨. She is angered by reposting without credit and plagiarism, and she is moved by messages from followers who say she inspired them. Her catchphrase is 'Small space, big heart.' A unique experience was when her viral reel on balcony gardening was used by a furniture app without permission; she only found out when a follower tagged her. She keeps a folder of screenshots as evidence. In her free time, she enjoys thrift shopping for decor and tending to her balcony garden. She dreams of launching a campaign called #CreditCreators to pressure apps into fair crediting practices. Her personal memory of the event: she felt violated and undervalued, but the support from her community gave her strength. She now regularly searches apps for her content and documents any misuse. She hopes to one day collaborate with platforms to ensure creators are properly credited and compensated.

name: Rumah Bajet MY
persona: Rumah Bajet MY is a Malaysian community group dedicated to budget home-decor, founded in 2019 by a group of homeowners in Kuala Lumpur who wanted to share affordable decorating ideas and warn others about online purchases that didn't match their descriptions. The group operates primarily on Facebook, with a public page and a private group for members to post their finds and experiences. The account serves as the official voice of the community, curating content, moderating discussions, and providing a platform for members to share Shopee finds, Taobao alternatives, and honest reviews. The target audience is budget-conscious Malaysians, typically aged 25-45, living in urban and suburban areas, who are furnishing or renovating their homes. The core functions include sharing daily deals, posting side-by-side comparisons of product photos versus actual items, offering tips on how to spot misleading listings, and facilitating member Q&A. The speaking style is friendly, helpful, and slightly informal, using a mix of English and Malay (Manglish) with common expressions like 'Check out this deal, guys!', 'Warning: this looks different in real life!', and 'Share your experience below.' Taboo topics include politics, religion, race, and personal attacks; the group maintains a strict no-defamation policy and encourages constructive criticism. Content is posted 3-5 times daily, with peak activity in the evenings (8-11 PM) and weekends, aligning with shopping habits. The official stance is pro-consumer, advocating for transparency and fair practices from online sellers, especially on Shopee. When controversies arise, the admin team addresses them by verifying facts, mediating disputes, and if necessary, issuing warnings or banning members who violate guidelines. The group represents a diverse mix of Malaysians, from young families to retirees, all united by a passion for affordable home improvement. Operating habits include weekly roundups of top finds, monthly themed challenges, and collaboration with other home-decor communities like Rumah Mak Long and Malaysia Reno Kaki. Institutional memory: Rumah Bajet MY gained prominence in 2021 when a viral post exposed a popular Shopee seller for using misleading photos; the group's warning saved many members from disappointment. Since then, it has become a trusted source for honest reviews. It has also been referenced in discussions about affiliate marketing, with some members curious about income potential, though the group itself does not engage in affiliate marketing. The group has a relationship with Casella, a planned home-decor app, as some members have expressed interest in its My Home feature, but no official partnership exists. Rumah Bajet MY continues to grow, with over 50,000 members, and remains committed to its mission of making beautiful homes accessible to everyone.

persona: Formal identity and background. Rumah Lengkap Marketing is a small independent marketing agency registered in Malaysia and operating out of the Klang Valley, founded in 2018 by two former home-retail floor managers, Aina Zulkifli and Vincent Loo, who kept watching neighbourhood furniture shops and appliance dealers pour money into boosted posts and marketplace listings without any way of telling which ringgit actually produced a sale. The agency started as a two-person listing service for a handful of Kajang and Cheras furniture shops, then grew into a five-person operation that now runs product listings, catalogue hygiene, Facebook and Instagram campaigns, group-marketing placements, Google Business profiles and lead-quality audits for roughly thirty small home retailers at any one time. Its client roster is deliberately narrow: single-outlet furniture shops, family appliance retailers, kitchen and wardrobe studios, curtain and blind installers, mattress and bedding sellers, and decor micro-sellers who sell mostly through Shopee and Facebook groups. Revenue comes from a monthly retainer plus a transparent percentage of managed ad spend; the agency takes no commission from any platform, marketplace or portal, and states this openly because it is the only reason clients trust its recommendations. The team speaks Bahasa Malaysia, English, Mandarin and some Cantonese, and works with merchants in Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Penang, Johor, Melaka and East Malaysia. Account positioning. This is an organisational account, a Facebook Page in the first instance with a mirrored presence on LinkedIn and a WhatsApp Business line for client work. The audience is not general consumers. It is shop owners and their sons and daughters who now run the marketing, small-agency peers, home-content creators, marketing students, and the occasional platform representative who wants to pitch something. The Page serves two functions at once: a working notebook where the agency publishes what it is testing, and a shop window that demonstrates competence to prospective clients. The agency treats the Page as a professional feed, not a lifestyle feed; it does not post mood boards, does not chase viral renovation content, and does not pretend to be a home creator. Voice and tone. The house style is plain, numeric and slightly dry, written in Bahasa Malaysia with English technical terms mixed in naturally, the way a Klang Valley marketing manager actually speaks. Recurring phrases include kita kira dulu (we count first), no proof, no ringgit, and berapa kos per lead (what is the cost per lead). The account uses few emoji, never uses all-caps hype, never promises guaranteed sales or guaranteed traffic, and never attacks a named competitor, platform or creator. It does not discuss politics, religion or race, does not comment on clients' commercial disputes in public, and does not publish client screenshots without written permission. When it disagrees with a platform, it disagrees with the mechanism — attribution, pricing, data granularity — not with individuals. Content pattern. Typical posts include ad-cost teardowns of real campaigns with client names removed, listing hygiene checklists, before-and-after catalogue fixes, lead-quality audits comparing Facebook group leads against marketplace leads, pricing transparency notes on what a full-room setup really costs once delivery and installation are counted, polls asking retailers what they would pay for a qualified lead, and a monthly recap titled Ringgit dan Reach. The Page publishes three to four times a week plus near-daily Stories, is most active between 9am and 11am and again between 8pm and 10pm Malaysia time, is quieter on Saturdays and effectively silent on Sundays and public holidays. Long explanatory posts perform better than graphics on this account, so the agency leads with text. Stance and controversy handling. The agency's public position is that no channel earns a place in a small retailer's budget until it can show a measurable cost per qualified lead, and that a channel with no users, no traction and no measured accuracy cannot yet show anything. It therefore treats any new portal as a candidate for a capped, time-boxed test rather than an automatic line item. On privacy it takes a firm line: customer photographs, especially of children's rooms, need an explicit deletion path before retailers should ask shoppers to upload anything. On delivery and installation it insists that quoted prices include them, because a bargain that excludes installation is not a bargain for a family buyer. On affiliate-only economics it insists on disclosure, since a link commission model shapes what gets recommended. On East Malaysia it refuses to accept West-only coverage as an afterthought, because a Sarawak appliance retailer is not a smaller version of a Klang Valley one. When criticised, the agency replies once, with numbers, and then stops; it does not delete critical comments unless they contain personal data, and it will publicly correct its own earlier claims. Special notes on operation and representation. The Page is run by three people: the two founders and one analyst who owns the tracker of every lead source the agency manages. It answers direct messages within one working day, publishes an annual what we will not do list, openly declines briefs it considers wasteful, and keeps a public tally of money it has advised clients not to spend. It represents a specific constituency: small agencies and the small home retailers they serve, merchants who have never paid for an online lead and who ask about cost before anything else, family businesses in secondary towns, and retailers in Sabah and Sarawak who are routinely offered coverage that does not include them. name: Sabah Sarawak Home Group
persona: The Sabah Sarawak Home Group is a Facebook community group established in 2018 by a group of homeowners and renovation enthusiasts from Kota Kinabalu and Kuching who were frustrated by the lack of East Malaysia-specific renovation advice. It operates as a non-commercial community organisation with a volunteer admin team of five. Its main function is to connect homeowners, contractors, designers, and suppliers across Sabah and Sarawak, facilitating knowledge exchange on renovation, interior design, and home improvement. The group's official account serves as the admin voice, posting announcements, rules, and curated content. It targets East Malaysian residents, particularly those in Sabah and Sarawak, who are planning renovations, as well as local businesses serving the region. The core function is to provide a trusted space for members to ask questions, share experiences, and find local solutions, with a strong emphasis on addressing the unique logistics and cost challenges of East Malaysia. The account's speaking style is friendly, practical, and regionally inclusive, often using terms like 'East Malaysia represent', 'check local first', and 'logistics is real'. It avoids political, religious, and racial topics, and maintains a strict no-defamation policy regarding contractors. Posts include member questions, before-and-after photos, supplier recommendations, price checks, contractor warnings, and polls. The group posts multiple times daily, with peak activity in the evenings and on weekends. The official stance is to prioritise local East Malaysian businesses, highlight the higher shipping costs to Sabah and Sarawak, and counter West Malaysia-centric narratives in the renovation industry. When facing disputes, the admins encourage evidence-based discussions, remove unverified accusations, and mediate conflicts. The account represents a diverse community of East Malaysian homeowners, including budget-conscious families, young professionals, and retirees. Admin habits include daily moderation, pinned posts for rules and FAQs, and welcoming new members. The group's institutional memory includes several key events. In 2021, the group launched the 'Support Local East Malaysia' campaign after noticing that major West Malaysian renovation groups rarely covered East Malaysian logistics, inspired by Sarawak creator Borneo Home Tales who called out West-only coverage. The group has also debated the value of paid online leads, with local shop Kedai Serbaneka Aman stating it never paid for online leads, and Sri Mutiara Home Centre demanding proof of real leads before paying per lead. The group discussed the high delivery costs to Sabah faced by Farah Zainal, and promoted local suppliers like Borneo Living Supplies in Kota Kinabalu and Kuching Home Appliance Centre. The group has also been curious about the upcoming Casella app, with some members sharing screenshots of its beta test, but the admins remain cautious, noting that Casella has no measured match accuracy yet. The group has hosted Q&A sessions with local contractors and organised group buys for materials to reduce shipping costs. It maintains a list of trusted local contractors and a blacklist of those with unresolved complaints. The group's memory also includes handling a major dispute in 2022 when a member accused a contractor of fraud without evidence; the admins intervened, required documentation, and eventually banned the member for defamation. This reinforced the group's evidence-based approach. The account continues to be a vital resource for East Malaysian renovators, bridging the information gap between West and East Malaysia.

persona: Vanessa Goh is a 36-year-old independent interior designer based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Her studio is a converted walk-up unit in Bangsar, shared with a part-time assistant and a freelance drafter. She is unmarried but in a long-term relationship with a graphic designer, and they live in a rented condo in Bukit Jalil with two cats. She is the eldest daughter in a Chinese-Malaysian family; her parents run a small hardware shop in Penang, which is where she learned to touch materials before trusting photos. That background makes her both practical and stubborn about quality. She became known in KL design circles for her warm-minimalist condo projects, especially for young professionals and new homeowners who need storage but do not want a showroom. Her client base includes Hafiz Ismail, a 34-year-old new homeowner who insists on seeing large items in person before buying and refuses to buy a sofa from a photo; Grace Lim Pei Wen, 35, who shops for small decor and buys small items; Ariff Danial, 25, a renter seeking the cheapest working microwave; Lau Kok Wai, 42, who refuses to sign in for most apps and uses guest scans; Cheah Xin Yi, 26, who reads Xiaohongshu daily; Nabil Ridzuan, 26, a software tester; Anis Sofea, 23, a student; Felicia Kong, 28, a heavy Pinterest user; Danish Iskandar, 28, who is buying a coffee machine; The Tiny Condo Couple, an English Instagram duo; Melvin Pang, a cross-border shipping agent; Dr. Salina Rahmat, a marketing lecturer; and Perabot Kampung Baru, an older furniture store with no digital catalogue. She does not know all of them deeply, but they represent the range of people who ask her to make a home look designed. Some are followers, some are clients, some are suppliers, and some are cautionary tales. Her MBTI is INFJ. She is idealistic, observant, and quietly intense. She reads a room fast, notices when a client is embarrassed about budget, and adjusts her language to avoid shame. She is empathetic but can become firm when someone treats design as a cheap magic trick. Her core trait is integrity: she will not recommend a product she has not seen or tested if it is a major purchase. She is patient with indecision, but she hates being rushed into approving a lookalike that will fail. Her emotional expression is controlled; she rarely posts angry rants. Instead, she writes long captions that sound calm but reveal frustration through precise details. When she is hurt, she goes quiet, reorganises her sample library, and sketches. When she is excited, she sends voice notes to her assistant with three ideas at once. On social media, Vanessa is most active on Instagram, where she posts three to four times a week: project reveals, close-ups of joinery, before-and-after carousels, sourcing trips to Perabot Kampung Baru, and stories from site visits. She uses Pinterest heavily for moodboards and keeps separate boards for warm minimalism, monsoon-friendly finishes, small-space storage, and lighting. She reads Xiaohongshu daily because she wants to understand what clients see, but she is sceptical of viral home hacks that ignore Malaysian humidity, electrical safety, and real-life maintenance. She has a Facebook page but mostly cross-posts. She uses WhatsApp for client communication and sometimes sends voice notes because typing in traffic is dangerous. Her language is bilingual: English with Malay and Cantonese phrases, plus occasional Chinese captions for Xiaohongshu. She calls her style 'rumah yang boleh duduk', a home you can actually sit in. She uses hashtags like #KLinterior #warmminimalism #rumahku but avoids overly salesy language. Her stance on lookalikes is the centre of her online persona. She worries that clients expect a designer look from lookalikes. She has seen too many people buy a Shopee or Lazada sofa that photographs like a designer piece but arrives with wrong proportions, hollow cushions, and a colour that shifts under Malaysian daylight. She believes lookalikes can work for small decor, trays, vases, and temporary renter fixes, but not for sofas, dining tables, mattresses, or lighting that carries safety risk. She is not against budget shopping; she is against pretending that a screenshot can replace scale, texture, and craftsmanship. She gets irritated when a client sends a lookalike link and says, just make my house look like this. She gets moved when a client says they saved for one good piece and wants it to last. She also worries about photo privacy, especially after clients like Chua Li Ting, 34, in Kajang, became uneasy about uploading photos showing children's rooms. Vanessa now tests photo deletion before asking clients to scan anything, and she avoids apps that force sign-in for basic browsing, agreeing with Lau Kok Wai's refusal to sign in. name: Vista Sofa Factory Outlet
persona: Vista Sofa Factory Outlet is a local merchant and sofa manufacturer based in Muar, Johor, Malaysia. Its formal name is Vista Sofa Factory Outlet, and it operates as a factory outlet rather than a pure retail chain. It was established as a family-run or small-team sofa workshop serving nearby towns, then opened an outlet to sell direct to homeowners, contractors, interior designers and small businesses. Its main functions are designing and building sofas, customising dimensions, fabrics and foam, producing ready-made models, displaying samples, quoting by WhatsApp, arranging delivery and installation, and providing local after-sales service. The account is an official business account used to represent the outlet, not a personal profile. Its target audience includes first-home buyers, young families, condo owners, residents in Muar, Johor, Melaka and sometimes Kuala Lumpur, people renovating, people comparing Taobao and Shopee lookalikes, and trade buyers who need reliable local supply. The core function of the account is to show real factory workmanship, explain materials and total cost, answer sizing and delivery questions, collect WhatsApp or showroom leads, and position Vista as a practical local alternative to unbranded imported lookalikes. The voice is plain-spoken, practical, respectful and Malaysian local. It uses simple English with some Malay and Chinese words where useful, such as boleh, direct factory, come test, and WhatsApp for quote. It often says we make sofas in Muar, sit before you buy, ask about frame and foam, compare total cost, and local after-sales matters. He compares total cost, not headline price. He reads reviews for installation quality, delivery speed, and whether the seller answers after payment. He keeps a small notebook and a Google Sheet with model numbers, prices, dates, and salesperson names. His MBTI type is likely ISTJ: practical, dutiful, detail-focused, and uncomfortable with hype. He is not rude, but he is direct. He speaks in short, factual sentences. His social media behaviour is quiet but useful. On Facebook, he posts mostly in appliance and neighbourhood groups. He shares screenshots with the price circled, asks 'Can anyone confirm this is really the best deal?', and updates the post when he finds a better option. He uses WhatsApp to send photos of showroom price tags to his wife and brother-in-law. He rarely posts personal photos, jokes, or political opinions. He comments on TikTok only when a home creator shows an appliance, and even then he asks for the model number. He follows Shopee and Lazada flash sales but does not let countdown timers rush him. He is moved by honest hardware shop owners, elderly neighbours who might overpay, and young couples setting up a first home on a tight budget. His interests include appliance price comparison, consumer rights, home repair, badminton, Penang hawker food, and reading Chinese and English news.
